summary: Provides an analysis grid for evaluating and comparing GMPLS capabilities against the recovery mechanisms proposed in the IETF CCAMP working group. It analyzes each recovery phase using the terminology of RFC 4427. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4428 provides a way to compare recovery mechanisms for GMPLS networks. It examines how failures are detected and reported, how traffic is moved to recovery paths, and how the network returns to normal.

subtitle: A framework for comparing how GMPLS networks detect failures, recover traffic, and restore normal paths.

tldr.problem: Several recovery mechanisms were proposed for GMPLS-controlled transport networks, and designers needed a common framework to compare how they behave.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes five recovery phases and compares mechanisms by convergence speed, switching time, robustness, and resource use.
tldr.outcome: The RFC concludes that the analyzed mechanisms call for GMPLS signaling extensions, while no GMPLS routing extensions are expected to be needed. It focuses on transport-plane recovery, not control-plane resilience.

today: RFC 4428 is an Informational RFC published in March 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it analyzes transport-plane recovery mechanisms rather than specifying a protocol.

sections.title: The Five Recovery Phases
sections.content:
The RFC analyzes mechanisms for recovering transport traffic when a label switched path (LSP) or span fails. It uses the terminology of RFC 4427 and considers failure detection, localization and isolation, notification, recovery, and reversion.

The first three activities are fault management. Recovery includes protection and restoration. The document focuses on SONET/SDH, Optical Transport Networks, and pre-OTN technologies, and does not analyze control-plane resilience.
sections.plainLanguage: Recovery begins by detecting a failure, locating it, and notifying the relevant devices. The network then moves traffic to a recovery path and may later return it to the repaired path.

sections.title: Detection, Localization, and Notification
sections.content:
Failure detection depends on the transport technology and cannot be done by the control plane alone. SONET/SDH supervision can detect loss of continuity, incorrect connectivity or alignment, a wrong payload type, and signal-quality problems; it reports Signal Degrade or Signal Fail conditions.

Localization identifies where the failure occurred. Notification informs intermediate nodes and the entities that decide or perform recovery. The RFC warns that too many notifications can overload the control plane, so alarms may need to be correlated, aggregated, and sent only to selected destinations.
sections.plainLanguage: The transport technology detects a failure, and the network identifies where it happened. Notifications need enough information to support recovery without flooding the control plane.

sections.title: Preparing Recovery Paths
sections.content:
A recovery path can be computed before a failure or on demand. A pre-computed path may be signaled before the failure to reserve resources, and those resources may also be selected in advance. More preparation can make switching faster, but it reserves resources and may limit which failures the path can handle.

Recovery capacity can be dedicated, shared among working paths, or left unreserved so restoration succeeds only if capacity is available. Dynamic restoration computes a path after a failure and is more flexible, but takes time to compute and reserve resources. The RFC also considers recovering an LSP segment instead of the entire end-to-end LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: Preparing a recovery path in advance can make switching faster but uses or reserves capacity. Finding a path after a failure is more flexible, but adds computation and setup time.

sections.title: Reversion, Hierarchies, and Diversity
sections.content:
Reversion moves traffic from a recovery path back to the repaired working path, if local policy enables it. A Wait-To-Restore timer requires the path to remain fault-free for a configurable period before traffic returns; the RFC gives a few minutes, such as 5 minutes, as an example. If the working path cannot be restored, its reserved resources must be released.

Recovery can be organized across different domains or network layers. Lower layers often switch faster, while higher layers can recover more specific traffic. A Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) identifies links that share a risk such as a fiber cable. Working and recovery paths need appropriate diversity because sharing a physical risk can make both paths fail together.
sections.plainLanguage: A repaired path may need to stay clear for a set time before traffic returns to it. Recovery paths should avoid the same physical risks as working paths.

sections.title: Comparing Mechanisms and Conclusions
sections.content:
The RFC compares recovery mechanisms by fast convergence, switching efficiency, robustness, and resource optimization. These goals can conflict: a dedicated protection path can recover quickly but use more capacity, while shared resources reduce capacity needs but may be less robust to simultaneous failures.

The RFC concludes that implementing the mechanisms requires attention to GMPLS signaling for pre-provisioning recovery paths, failure notification, switching, and reversion. It does not expect GMPLS routing extensions to be needed for the recovery types and schemes it analyzes.
sections.plainLanguage: Recovery designs trade speed and resilience against the amount of spare capacity they use. The RFC says the mechanisms need signaling support, but not new GMPLS routing extensions.

sections.title: Authorization of Recovery Resources
sections.content: The RFC introduces no additional security issue for the GMPLS protocols it discusses. It notes that local policy should decide whether an authenticated requester may use network resources, especially when recovery resources are shared or dynamically selected.
sections.plainLanguage: Network policy must determine who may use recovery resources. This matters when several paths share spare capacity.
